    This is an estimate for planning. It covers federal income tax, FICA, and simplified state income tax. It does not include local or paid-leave taxes. Your employer's payroll system may calculate a different amount.

    Does Michigan have a state income tax?

    Yes. Michigan taxes wage income at one flat rate instead of graduated brackets. For the 2026 tax year the Department of Treasury set that rate at 4.25%, which applies to every dollar of taxable income once the personal exemption is subtracted. Michigan briefly fell to 4.05% in 2023 under a revenue-trigger formula in the Income Tax Act, but the trigger did not fire again and the rate returned to 4.25%.

    The calculator on this page applies the flat 4.25% rate after the Michigan standard deduction used in the 2026 data ($5,600 for a single filer). Michigan’s actual personal exemption is $5,900 per person for 2026, so the state line here is a close estimate; your employer withholds using the state’s own tables and Form MI-W4.

    How Michigan take-home pay is calculated

    1. Gross pay. Your annual salary, or hourly rate times hours worked, converted to the pay period you selected.
    2. Pre-tax deductions. 401(k), HSA, and health premiums come out first, so they lower the income that Michigan and federal tax are charged on.
    3. Michigan income tax. A flat 4.25% for 2026 is charged on taxable wages after the state standard deduction, with no bracket tiers to climb.
    4. Federal income tax. The federal standard deduction is applied, then the federal marginal brackets.
    5. FICA. Social Security at 6.2% (up to the wage base) and Medicare at 1.45%, plus the 0.9% additional Medicare tax above the high-earner threshold.
    6. City income tax (not included). Residents of the 24 Michigan cities with a local income tax owe a separate city tax. This calculator does not subtract it.

    The result is your net pay for the period you selected. Pay frequency matters: a biweekly schedule pays 26 times a year and a semi-monthly schedule 24, so the same salary produces different per-paycheck amounts.

    Worked example: $60,000 in Michigan

    A single filer earning $60,000 a year, paid bi-weekly in 2026:

    LinePer paycheck
    Gross pay$2,307.69
    Federal income tax$193.08
    Social Security$143.08
    Medicare$33.46
    Michigan state income tax$88.92
    Net take-home pay$1,849.15

    That is $48,078.00 a year, an effective tax rate of about 19.9%. Change the inputs in the calculator above to see your own numbers.

    How Michigan compares

    Michigan sits in the middle of the state-tax pack. Its 4.25% flat rate is higher than Ohio’s graduated rates for lower earners and close to Illinois’ 4.95% flat rate, but far below California’s graduated schedule and far above zero-tax states like Texas, Florida, and Washington. A flat rate also means a high earner and an average earner pay the same percentage on each taxable dollar.

    What separates Michigan from most flat-tax states is the city layer. Detroit residents pay a 2.4% city income tax and Detroit nonresidents who work in the city pay 1.2%; Grand Rapids charges residents 1.5% and nonresidents 0.75%. Cities act under the City Income Tax Act (Act 284 of 1964), and the Department of Treasury lists 24 cities that levy an income-related tax. None of that city tax appears on the state line, so a Detroit paycheck nets less than the state-only estimate here.

    FAQ

    Does Michigan have a state income tax?

    Yes. Michigan taxes wage income at a flat 4.25% for the 2026 tax year. There are no graduated brackets; the same rate applies to every dollar of taxable income after the personal exemption is subtracted.

    What is the Michigan income tax rate for 2026?

    Michigan's flat individual income tax rate is 4.25% for the 2026 tax year, as set by the Department of Treasury after applying the revenue-trigger formula in the Income Tax Act.

    How much is taken out of a $60,000 salary in Michigan?

    For 2026, a single filer paid biweekly takes home about $1,849.15 per paycheck from a $60,000 salary: $2,307.69 gross, $193.08 federal income tax, $143.08 Social Security, $33.46 Medicare, and $88.92 Michigan state income tax. A city income tax such as Detroit's is not included.

    Do Michigan cities charge their own income tax?

    Yes. Twenty-four Michigan cities levy an income-related municipal tax under the City Income Tax Act. Detroit residents pay 2.4% and Detroit nonresidents 1.2%, while Grand Rapids charges residents 1.5% and nonresidents 0.75%. Other cities on the list include Lansing, Flint, Saginaw, Pontiac, Jackson, and Muskegon.

    How does the Michigan personal exemption work?

    Michigan grants a personal exemption that is subtracted before the flat rate is applied. For 2026 the exemption is $5,900 per person, and it is claimed through Form MI-W4 with your employer. The simplified state data used by this calculator uses $5,600, so treat the state figure here as an estimate.

    Does Michigan have a state disability or paid family leave payroll tax?

    No. Michigan does not operate a state disability insurance program or a state paid family leave program, so no state payroll tax for either is withheld from a Michigan paycheck.

    What withholding form does a Michigan employee file?

    A Michigan employee files Form MI-W4 with their employer to set state income tax withholding. It is separate from the federal Form W-4 and controls how the state personal exemption is applied to each paycheck.

    Why did the Michigan income tax rate change a few years ago?

    Michigan's Income Tax Act contains a formula that lowers the flat rate when general fund revenue exceeds a trigger threshold. That happened for tax year 2023, when the rate fell to about 4.05%. The trigger did not repeat, so the rate returned to 4.25% and remains there for 2026.
